title: Construction and lifetime completion
lead: Trace construction of object parts and automatic cleanup in reverse order.
why: A constructor establishes an object's initial state. Its name matches the class and it has no return type. In Level(int n):value_(n), the part after the colon is a member initializer list. The field is created with n directly. Assignment inside the body happens later, after the member has already had to be created.
objectives: Explain why Lease copying is forbidden.
prerequisites: Modules 1–4: input, functions, sequences, ownership, testing and multifile builds.

sections.title: Initialization precedes the body
paragraphs: A constructor establishes an object's initial state. Its name matches the class and it has no return type. In Level(int n):value_(n), the part after the colon is a member initializer list. The field is created with n directly. Assignment inside the body happens later, after the member has already had to be created.

Prefer direct initialization, especially for const members, references and types without a default constructor. An uninitialized built-in int can hold an indeterminate value that must not be read. A =0 field initializer supplies a useful default, but does not replace validation of domain requirements on constructor arguments.

sections.title: Declaration order controls initialization
paragraphs: Members are initialized in their declaration order inside the class, regardless of their order in the initializer list. The constructor body executes afterwards. Machine therefore creates a, then b, then prints ready. Rearranging a and b in the initializer list is not a way to change their lifetimes.

If the second member needs the first during construction, declare the dependency earlier. Fix a compiler warning about reordered initialization instead of ignoring it. Do not demonstrate the rule by reading a member whose lifetime has not begun. A safe trace prints identifiers of initialized parts and reveals order without undefined behaviour.

sections.title: Explicit construction and caller intent
paragraphs: A one-argument constructor can participate in an implicit conversion when its declaration permits it. explicit prevents that copy-initialization conversion while allowing an explicit Level{7}. Calling show(l) with an existing Level is clear; show(7) in the negative example must fail to compile.

This matters for units, identifiers and resources: the integer seven should not accidentally become seven metres or an opened handle. explicit neither checks a range nor automatically makes a type safe. Separate the decisions about permitted conversions from the decisions about which values satisfy the construction contract.

sections.title: Destruction reverses construction
paragraphs: A destructor is spelled ~Type() and has no parameters. Automatic objects are destroyed in reverse order of successful construction when their scope ends. The complete object's destructor body runs first, followed by its members in reverse declaration order. The Machine trace therefore ends with stop, minus B, minus A.

Reverse order follows dependencies: a later part may rely on an earlier part and should finish first. Do not manually call the destructor of an ordinary local object; later automatic destruction would make the program incorrect. Scopes, containers and standard-library owners suffice for ordinary course work. Placement new is outside this lesson's requirements.

sections.title: Owning a resource counter
paragraphs: Lease stores an int& referring to an external active counter. Its constructor increments it and its destructor decrements it. The counter outlives every Lease because it is declared earlier in an outer scope. A reference does not own the integer or extend its lifetime. That is an important precondition of this teaching model.

Copying Lease is deleted with =delete. Otherwise two copies could decrement a counter after just one original increment, violating ownership accounting. We do not implement a custom move yet; that has a separate lesson. A deleted operation is a compile-time prohibition rather than a special result produced while the program runs.

sections.title: Tracing a nested scope
paragraphs: With mode zero, only a exists: the output contains one inside the scope, one before its end and zero afterwards. With mode one, b is created too; one, two, one, zero shows that b is destroyed after the inner if and a later. Mode two intentionally follows the same path and checks the stated input contract.

Write an event, live-object and active-count table before running. The counter is not a universal memory leak detector, but checks acquire/release pairing in this model. Do not inspect a destroyed b to discover what happened; observe the counter whose lifetime continues. No Lease owners remain after the outer scope ends.

sections.title: Construction failure and cleanup
paragraphs: If construction of a complete object fails with an exception, that complete object's destructor is not called. Members that were successfully constructed are cleaned up. Throwing is studied later; the design implication already matters: do not leave ownership in an unprotected raw pointer between constructor steps.

Destructors should finish without throwing exceptions. Output in tracing examples makes order visible; it is not a model for complicated cleanup with recoverable failures. Handle a file-saving error in an explicit operation before destruction. Prefer established RAII owners for real resources because they reduce the number of manual release paths.

sections.title: Laboratory and transfer
paragraphs: Save the Lease source and traces for all three permitted modes. Explain declaration order, the beginning of lifetime, scope exit and destruction order as separate events. Change nesting safely and predict the new sequence first. Invalid input must be rejected before any Lease objects are created.

The cumulative Window practicum combines the invariant with initialization of an empty interval. Resource discipline next transfers to unique_ptr and standard containers. The goal is not to write a destructor for every class. When members already manage their resources, a user-written destructor is often unnecessary.
